data.text/markdown:
Shortest paths in graphs (Dijkstra)

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to find shortest paths in a topological map: a graph whose nodes are places and whose edges join places that can be traveled between directly. It uses two MRPT modules:
  • mrpt.poses: SE(2) poses (CPose2D) and the relative pose between two of them, b - a.
  • mrpt.graphs: the graph (CNetworkOfPoses2D) and Dijkstra's algorithm on it (dijkstra_path, dijkstra_tree, getNodeDistances).
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest path from a source node to every other node, given a non-negative cost for each edge. The cost decides what "shortest" means: with one per edge, the path with fewest edges; with the length of each edge, the path with the shortest distance. Move the sliders: everything below is recomputed.

data.text/markdown:
1. A random topological map

The nodes are random poses in a 30 m × 30 m area, and every pair of nodes closer than the link radius is joined by an edge. As in a pose graph, an edge i → j stores the pose of node j relative to node i; its length is edge.norm(). Dijkstra in mrpt.graphs ignores the direction of the edges, so one edge per pair is enough.

data.text/markdown:
2. Two meanings of "shortest"

dijkstra_path(source, target) returns the list of node IDs of the cheapest path. By default each edge costs 1, so it finds the path with fewest edges. Its optional edge_weight argument is a function (from_id, to_id, edge) -> cost; with lambda a, b, edge: edge.norm() the cost is the metric distance. The C++ class behind both, mrpt::graphs::CDijkstra, takes the same kind of function.

Edge cost Path from node 0 to node 18 Edges Length (m)
Fewest edges (default) [0, 2, 18] 2 20.5
Metric distance (edge_weight=metric) [0, 4, 15, 18] 3 14.6
The straight-line distance between both nodes is 14.4 m.

3. The shortest-path tree

Dijkstra does not compute a single path: it finds the cheapest path from the source to every reachable node at once. Together, these paths form a spanning tree rooted at the source. dijkstra_tree(source, edge_weight) returns it as a dict {node: parent}, and getNodeDistances(source, edge_weight) the cost of reaching each node. Switch the edge cost above to see how the tree changes.

4. Traversing the tree

The C++ example graphs_dijkstra_example prints this tree with depth-first and breadth-first traversals. With the {node: parent} dict, both are a few lines of Python:
